subject: technology
essential_question: What does it mean to defend your own work honestly, including its limits?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Impacts of Computing
project_brief: Defend the capstone in a chosen private or public mode with complete documentation, a response to independent review, and a maintenance and transition plan. This is the grade 12 culminating project for "Capstone Review, Defense, and Transition" (ma-g12-technology-u06, unit 6), built around evidence assembly and documentation, independent review and critique response, limitations and future work, maintenance security and sunset planning, and presentation in a chosen private or public mode. Defend the capstone in a chosen private or public mode with complete documentation, a response to independent review, and a maintenance and transition plan. Use only fictional examples, sandbox tools, or already-approved data — never a real account, real credential, or live external system.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: evidence assembly and documentation, independent review and critique response, limitations and future work, maintenance security and sunset planning, presentation in a chosen private or public mode, and pathways portfolio and transition.
Meet the performance task as written: Defend the capstone in a chosen private or public mode with complete documentation, a response to independent review, and a maintenance and transition plan.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Defend the capstone in a chosen private or public mode with complete documentation, a response to independent review, and a maintenance and transition plan. Use only fictional examples, sandbox tools, or already-approved data — never a real account, real credential, or live external system.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to evidence assembly and documentation or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering evidence assembly and documentation in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to independent review and critique response, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
